blocks.text: An MCP server rarely just sits there waiting to be told what to do. Many servers ship with a set of ready made prompt templates, ones the author already knows work well for common tasks, and a client needs a reliable way to find out what those templates are.

That mechanism is prompt discovery, built around a single request called prompts/list. It is the same basic idea as listing tools or resources, but the payload describes reusable pieces of conversation starter rather than callable functions or readable files.

This lesson walks through the request and response shape, the metadata that makes a prompt usable, when discovery happens, and how a host application turns a plain list of prompts into something a user can actually click or type.
1. What Prompt Discovery Solves
A client connecting to a brand new MCP server has no idea what prompts, if any, that server offers. It cannot read the server code, and it should not have to guess.
Prompt discovery gives the client a single, standard question to ask, and a standard shaped answer back, so any client can work with any server without custom integration work.
This matters just as much for a human using a chat style host as it does for a model deciding, on its own, whether a prompt template might help with the current task.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Without a discovery step, a server would need some out of band way to tell every possible client about its prompts, which does not scale and breaks the whole point of a shared protocol.

blocks.text: 2. The prompts/list Request
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697454-139569088.png
The client sends a plain JSON-RPC request named prompts/list. It carries no required arguments beyond the standard envelope, since the client is simply asking for everything the server has.
An empty params object is normal here. Some servers accept an optional cursor field for pagination, covered later in this lesson, but a first call typically omits it entirely.
The method name itself, prompts/list, follows the same namespaced pattern used across MCP, matching tools/list and resources/list so a client can guess the shape before ever reading a spec.
3. The prompts/list Response
The server answers with a result containing a prompts array. Each entry is a small metadata object describing one reusable template, not the template text itself.

Notice the response describes the prompt, it does not include the actual instructions the server will later assemble. That text only appears when the client calls prompts/get, a separate step covered in another lesson.
4. Prompt Metadata Fields
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697454-603338311.png
Each prompt entry carries three pieces of metadata, and together they are everything a client needs to decide whether and how to offer that prompt to a user.

items: name, a short stable identifier used to actually request the prompt later
description, a plain sentence explaining what the prompt is for
arguments, an array describing any inputs the prompt needs, each with its own name, description, and required flag

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose","Example"],"rows":[["name","Identifier passed to prompts/get","summarize_pull_request"],["description","Human readable explanation shown to a user","Summarize the changes in a pull request for a reviewer"],["arguments","What inputs the prompt needs before it can run","pr_number, required; tone, optional"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Why Description Text Matters So Much
A description is not decoration, it is often the only thing standing between a user and total confusion about what a prompt does. A vague description like process data tells a user nothing useful.

A good description names the concrete task and the expected outcome, something like draft a friendly reply to a support ticket, so a user can decide in one glance whether it fits what they are trying to do.
When a model, rather than a person, is the one browsing the catalog, the same rule applies even more strongly, since the model has nothing to go on besides that one line of text.
6. Argument Metadata in Detail
6.1 Required vs Optional Arguments
An argument marked required must be supplied before prompts/get can succeed, while an optional argument can be left out and the server falls back to some sensible default.
6.2 Argument Descriptions Guide the Host
The description on an argument is what a host uses to label a form field or a slash command placeholder, so a user filling it in knows exactly what value is expected.
7. Listing at Session Start

Most clients call prompts/list once, right after the connection handshake finishes, and cache the result for the rest of the session. This lets a host build its whole slash command menu before a user has typed anything at all.
Calling it early also means a user never hits a moment where they type a slash command that the host has not yet learned exists, since the catalog is already loaded.
8. Listing on Demand

A client is also free to call prompts/list again at any later point, not just at startup. This is useful if a client suspects the catalog might have changed, or simply wants a fresh copy before showing a picker.
Some hosts choose a hybrid approach, an eager call at connection time for instant availability, plus an on demand refresh triggered by a user action like opening a prompt browser.
An on demand call is also the safe fallback for any server that never advertises listChanged support, since the client cannot otherwise be sure its cached copy is still accurate.
9. The prompts/list_changed Notification
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697684-78440270.png
A server whose prompt catalog can change after startup, say an admin adds a new template, sends a notification named prompts/list_changed rather than expecting the client to keep polling.
This message carries no payload describing what changed, it is purely a signal. On receiving it, a well behaved client calls prompts/list again to fetch the current, complete catalog.
10. Why a Diff Is Not Sent

blocks.alt: Why a Diff Is Not Sent
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697685-366669038.png

It might seem more efficient for the notification to include exactly which prompt was added or removed, but MCP deliberately keeps it minimal. A full relist is simple, always correct, and avoids the hard problem of keeping incremental diffs in sync.
For a catalog of a few dozen prompts, refetching the whole list is cheap enough that the simplicity is worth far more than the small bandwidth saving a diff would offer.
11. Declaring the Capability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697685-737687702.png

A server only advertises prompts/list_changed support if it actually intends to send that notification. This is declared during capability negotiation at connection time, covered in its own earlier lesson.
A client checks this flag before deciding whether it can rely on notifications, or whether it needs to relist proactively every so often instead.
12. Surfacing Prompts as Slash Commands
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697686-717715065.png
The most common way a host application presents discovered prompts to a user is as slash commands, typed shortcuts that start with a forward slash followed by the prompt name.

This mirrors a pattern many users already know from chat tools and editors, so a discovered prompt named summarize_pull_request naturally becomes something the user can type as slash summarize_pull_request.
13. Prompting the User for Arguments
Once a user picks a slash command, the host still needs values for any required arguments before it can call prompts/get. A simple approach parses them inline, a richer host pops up a small form.
14. Grouping and Filtering Discovered Prompts

A server offering dozens of prompts can make its catalog hard to browse, so many hosts group entries by a naming convention or a category hint, and offer a simple search box over the description text.

items: Group by a common name prefix, like git_ prompts versus docs_ prompts
Let a user type a few letters to filter the slash command list live
Show the most recently used prompts first, ahead of the full alphabetical list

blocks.text: 15. Pagination for Large Prompt Catalogs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697686-489278014.png
A server with a very large number of prompts may return results a page at a time, using the same cursor pattern seen elsewhere in MCP listing methods.
A client keeps calling prompts/list with the returned cursor until no nextCursor comes back, at which point it has the complete catalog.
17. Keeping Discovery Fast and Cheap
A prompts/list call should be fast, since a host may run it every time a connection opens, sometimes several times a session if the user reconnects.
A server that computes its prompt catalog dynamically should keep that computation lightweight, static in memory metadata rather than an expensive database scan on every single call.

blocks.title: Practical tip
blocks.content: If building the catalog really is expensive, compute it once at server startup and only rebuild it when something that would actually change the list happens, then fire prompts/list_changed.

blocks.text: 18. Worked Example

Picture a documentation MCP server for an engineering team. At connection time, the client sends prompts/list and gets back three entries, explain_error_code, write_changelog_entry, and draft_migration_guide.

The host turns each into a slash command, so a user typing slash draft in their editor sees draft_migration_guide suggested immediately, complete with its description and its two arguments, from_version and to_version.

A week later, an engineer adds a fourth prompt, summarize_breaking_changes, directly on the server. The server fires prompts/list_changed, the client relists, and the new slash command appears without anyone restarting the editor.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing a description so vague, like helper prompt, that a user cannot tell what the prompt actually does
Forgetting to declare listChanged support even though the server does send the notification later
Treating prompts/list_changed as if it carries details of exactly what changed, when it is only a signal to relist
Only listing prompts once at startup and never again, so a later catalog change is invisible to the user
Leaving argument descriptions blank, forcing a user to guess what value a slash command placeholder expects
Building a slash command menu that ignores the required flag, letting a user submit a prompt missing a value it truly needs

blocks.text: Practice
Design the prompts/list response for a server that offers a single prompt named triage_bug_report, taking a required severity argument and an optional assignee argument.
Key Takeaway
Prompt discovery is a small, predictable exchange, prompts/list out, a metadata array back, that lets any client learn what reusable templates a server offers without ever seeing the server source.
Good metadata, clear names, honest descriptions, well labeled arguments, is what turns that raw list into slash commands a user can actually understand and use with confidence.
